property_summary: For every calldata layout produced by the factory cloning (i.e., for any immutable args block), the correct contract's owner() always reads the first immutable address slot at offset 0x00 while the mutant that reads offset 0x04 can return a different address for some immutable-args layouts (i.e., owner() must equal the address read at offset 0x00 for all inputs, which the mutant can violate).

For any calldata layout of immutable args, owner() returns the address stored at immutable offset 0x00; the mutant reading offset 0x04 can return a different address for some immutable-args layouts and thus violate this equality.

For any immutable-args calldata layout, C.owner() always returns the 20-byte address located at immutable offset 0x00 (the first immutable address); the mutant reading offset 0x04 can return a different address for some calldata, so there exists calldata for which owner() differs.

For every immutable-args calldata layout, C.owner() returns the address located at immutable offset 0x00; the mutant that reads offset 0x04 can return a different address for some immutable-data, so there exist inputs (different immutable-data bytes) where owner() differs between correct and mutant.

For any calldata layout of immutable args (bytes), C.owner() returns the address encoded at immutable offset 0x00; the mutant that reads offset 0x04 will for some immutable-args bytes return a different address, so owner() must equal the address decoded from offset 0x00 for all admissible bytes but the mutant can violate this.

For any input, the genuine contract's owner() must return the immutable owner address embedded at arg offset 0x0 (i.e. a nonzero address when the deployed clone was initialized with a nonzero owner); the mutant returning address(0) violates this rule for any clone whose embedded owner is nonzero.

For any bytes32 ownerArg value used as the first immutable arg when deploying the clone implementation, the reference contract's owner() returns that exact (nonzero) address; the mutant returns address(0) instead and thus differs for any nonzero embedded owner.

For any nonzero address implanted as the clone's first immutable argument, C.owner() returns that implanted address; the mutant returns address(0) instead, so for any nonzero implanted owner the mutant's return differs.

For any address arg placed as the first immutable argument of the clone, the reference C.owner() returns that embedded address (i.e. owner() equals the immutable-owner stored in calldata), whereas the mutant returns address(0) and thus differs for some nonzero embedded owner.

For any (possibly zero) address input treated as the owner immutable arg embedded in a clone's calldata, the reference C.owner() returns that embedded address; the mutant returns address(0) instead, so for some nonzero embedded owner the returned value differs.

For any calldata embedding of cloned immutable args, collateral() always returns the embedded address at offset 0x14 (i.e. the second embedded address) whereas the mutant reading offset 0x0 will sometimes return a different address (breaking the equality), so the reference always returns an address different from owner() when the two embedded addresses differ and the mutant can return owner() instead.

For any calldata layout used by the clone, collateral() always returns the embedded collateral address at its intended offset (the second embedded address), so collateral() != owner() whenever the embedded collateral address differs from the embedded owner address; the mutant that reads the wrong offset can return owner() instead, violating this relation for some inputs.

For any deployed C clone, collateral() returns the second embedded address (the collateral ERC20) which is distinct from the owner() (first embedded address) whenever those two embedded addresses differ; the mutant reading the wrong offset can return the owner() instead, so there exists inputs where collateral() == owner() for the mutant but never for the correct contract when embedded addresses differ.

For any deployed C instance (constructed via new C()), the public getter collateral() always returns some address (an ERC20); specifically, collateral() never equals owner() for those inputs where the embedded collateral and owner addresses differ in calldata for a properly constructed clone — the mutant that reads the wrong offset can make collateral() equal owner(), so the rule is that collateral() != owner() for any C created by new C() (with no special calldata embedding), and the mutant breaks this for some inputs when calldata embeds different addresses at the two offsets.

For the correct contract, calling collateral() on a freshly deployed C (via new C()) is a pure call that does not revert and returns an address; the mutant that reads the wrong immutable-arg offset can produce a different address or revert behavior when fed arbitrary calldata via a low-level staticcall to collateral() — therefore the invariant is: collateral() callable via try/catch always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference for any calldata length, while the mutant can cause a differing return (or revert) for some calldata, so try/catch success must be true for all inputs on the reference but not for the mutant.

For any calldata layout produced by Clone-based creation, collateral() returns the address encoded as the second immutable argument (offset 0x14); the mutant that reads at 0x28 will return a different address whenever the second and third encoded addresses differ, breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any two distinct addresses A and B passed as the 2nd and 3rd immutable args to the clone, the reference contract's collateral() always returns the 2nd encoded address (A); the mutant that reads one word later will sometimes return the 3rd address (B), so there exists inputs where collateral() differs.

For any two distinct addresses encoded as the 2nd and 3rd immutable constructor args of the clone, the correct contract's collateral() always returns the 2nd encoded address; the mutant that reads one word later will sometimes return the 3rd address, so there exist fuzzed address pairs where collateral() differs.

For any two addresses provided as the 2nd and 3rd immutable args when a clone is created, the reference C's collateral() always returns the 2nd encoded address; the mutant that reads one word later may return the 3rd encoded address, so there exist fuzzed address inputs where collateral() differs between reference and mutant.

For any two distinct addresses passed as the 2nd and 3rd immutable args to a clone of C, the reference C.collateral() always returns the 2nd encoded address (the collateral arg); the mutant that reads one word later will return the 3rd encoded address for some inputs, so there exist fuzzed address pairs where collateral() differs.
For any deployed C, collateral() must return a non-zero ERC20 address equal to the immutable argument embedded at deployment; the mutant returns address(0) breaking this invariant for some inputs.
For any deployed reference C, collateral() returns a non-zero ERC20 address (the immutable arg); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For any deployed C, calling collateral() should return a non-zero address derived from immutable args (so collateral() != address(0)); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any deployed C, calling collateral() returns an ERC20 whose address, when used as an argument to SafeTransferLib.safeTransferFrom (i.e. as the token target) results in a call that does not revert when the token address is a contract (non-zero) — the reference returns the embedded contract address so a subsequent safeTransferFrom to that address can succeed/fail based on that contract, while the mutant returns address(0) which makes collateral() address equal to address(0) and thus calls that expect a token contract will behave differently (low-level call to address(0) will fail), so there exist fuzzed inputs that distinguish them; the test drives collateral() through an external call and asserts the call succeeded for the reference for all fuzzed params but can fail under the mutant for some params.

For any deployed C, calling collateral() returns a non-zero address (the immutable arg) so invoking collateral().decimals() via the ERC20 interface succeeds (does not revert); the mutant returns address(0) causing a call to decimals() to revert for some fuzzed inputs, breaking the rule.

For any calldata (i.e. for all deployed clone immutable args), the correct contract's collateral() returns the ERC20 address stored at immutable arg offset 0x14, whereas the mutant returns the factory address located at offset 0x3c — so the property: collateral() == ERC20(_getArgAddress(0x14)) always holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant for inputs where the values at offsets 0x14 and 0x3c differ.

For every input, the correct contract's collateral() returns the address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14 (the collateral token); the mutant returns the address at offset 0x3c (factory) instead, so whenever the two encoded addresses differ the mutant will return a different value and violate this rule.

For any deployed C instance, collateral() returns the address encoded in immutable arg offset 0x14; the mutant reads offset 0x3c instead, so when the two immutable-encoded addresses differ the mutant returns a different value and thus violates this property.

For any deployed C instance, collateral() returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14; the mutant reads offset 0x3c instead, so when the two encoded addresses differ the mutant returns a different address and violates this rule.

For any deployed C, collateral() always returns a non-zero ERC20 address (the collateral token) encoded in the clone immutables; the mutant returns the factory address instead for some deployments (when the immutables at offsets 0x14 and 0x3c differ), so there exists inputs where collateral() differs — we assert that collateral() is not equal to factory(), which holds for the reference for all admissible fuzzed factory/collateral inputs where they differ but the mutant will match factory() and thus violate the property for those inputs.

For any deployed C clone, the debt() getter always returns the immutable clone argument stored at the 0x28 slot; the mutant that reads 0x2c will return a different address for some immutable-data layouts (so the returned ERC20 address differs).

For any clone instance produced from C's correct implementation, calling debt() always returns the ERC20 address stored at the immutable slot corresponding to the debt argument (offset 0x28); the mutant reads a different immutable slot (0x2c) and thus for some immutable data layouts the returned address differs, breaking the equality between the two retrieved addresses when the clone's immutable layout places distinct addresses at 0x28 and 0x2c.

For any deployed C instance constructed with immutable args where two adjacent immutable slots differ, calling debt() returns the address encoded in the correct immutable slot (0x28); the mutant reads a different slot (0x2c) so for some immutable calldata layouts debt() returns a different address and thus the equality between the expected slot and returned address is violated.

For any two distinct addresses A and B used as adjacent immutable args in the clone creation data (owner at 0x00, collateral at 0x14, debt at 0x28, factory at 0x3c), the reference contract's debt() always returns the address placed at the 0x28 immutable slot (the debt address), whereas the mutant reads the 0x2c slot and thus will return a different address when the immutable words at 0x28 and 0x2c differ.

For any C instance constructed with immutable args, the reference's debt() always returns the ERC20 address encoded at the immutable slot for debt (offset 0x28); the mutant that reads offset 0x2c can return a different address when the immutables at 0x28 and 0x2c differ, so the equality between debt() and the address read from the canonical slot is violated for some inputs.

For any deployed C, debt() returns the ERC20 located at the immutable arg offset for the debt address (the third immutable arg); the mutant returns the owner immutable arg instead, so for inputs where owner != debt the returned address differs and the property is violated.
